# opencode-openrgb

Ambient status lighting for [opencode](https://opencode.ai), driven by
[OpenRGB](https://openrgb.org).

Your RGB hardware mirrors what opencode is doing: amber while the agent works,
violet when it is waiting on a permission prompt, red when something fails. When
everything goes idle, your original lighting is restored exactly as it was.

There are no model-facing tools. The plugin never lets the LLM touch your
lights — it only reacts to session state.

| State        | Meaning                                  | Default   |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------- | --------- |
| `busy`       | at least one session is working          | `#ff8c00` |
| `retry`      | a request is being retried               | `#ffd000` |
| `permission` | a permission prompt is waiting for you   | `#b400ff` |
| `error`      | a session errored (decays after 10s)     | `#ff0000` |
| `idle`       | nothing running                          | restore   |

Any state can instead be set to `"baseline"`, meaning *your own* lighting,
breathing. See [Pulsing your own color](#pulsing-your-own-color).

State is aggregated across **all** sessions, so subagent and task work keeps the
lights busy until everything is genuinely finished. When several conditions hold
at once, the highest priority wins: `error` > `permission` > `retry` > `busy` >
`idle`.

## Requirements

- OpenRGB running with its SDK server enabled (Settings → General → *Enable SDK
  Server*), listening on `127.0.0.1:6742` by default
- opencode 2.0+

Protocol versions 1–5 are supported; the client negotiates `min(server, 5)`.

> This plugin targets the opencode 2 plugin API and does not load under 1.x.

## Install

```sh
opencode plugin add @tiuxo/opencode-openrgb
```

The plugin only loads for projects whose config declares it. For ambient
lighting everywhere, declare it **globally** in
`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugins": ["@tiuxo/opencode-openrgb"]
}
```

Config is hot-reloaded, so the plugin activates on save. Use `/reload` to force
it.

### From source

Clone the repository and point `package` at the directory, using an absolute
path — plugin paths resolve relative to the config file that declares them:

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugins": [
    { "package": "/absolute/path/to/opencode-openrgb" }
  ]
}
```

Point it at the repository directory, not a file inside it: opencode skips
configured plugin paths that are not directories.

To check what the plugin can see before enabling it:

```sh
bun run probe
```

## Options

Every field is optional. Invalid values log a warning and fall back to the
default rather than failing to load.

```jsonc
{
  "package": "@tiuxo/opencode-openrgb",
  "options": {
    "enabled": true,
    "host": "127.0.0.1",
    "port": 6742,

    "colors": {
      // A hex/named color, or "baseline" to breathe your own lighting.
      "busy": "#ff8c00",
      "retry": "#ffd000",
      "permission": "#b400ff",
      "error": "#ff0000"
    },

    // "restore" puts back the lighting captured at startup.
    // A color instead holds that color while idle. "off" goes dark.
    "idle": "restore",

    "brightness": 1.0,     // 0..1, applied in software
    "pulse": false,        // breathing effect while busy
    "pulseFps": 15,

    "debounceMs": 120,     // coalesce bursts of events
    "restoreDelayMs": 400, // extra settle time before handing control back

    "devices": {
      "include": ["motherboard", "dram", "gpu", "cooler", "case", "ledstrip"],
      "exclude": []
    },

    "debug": false
  }
}
```

Colors accept `#rgb`, `#rrggbb`, `rgb(r, g, b)`, and names like `amber`,
`violet`, `off`.

### Pulsing your own color

If you would rather not have a status color replace your carefully chosen
lighting, set a state to `"baseline"`:

```jsonc
{ "colors": { "busy": "baseline" } }
```

The device then breathes *its own* color while the agent works — whatever the
lighting was when the plugin connected — so your OpenRGB profile keeps its
identity and only its intensity changes. This is per LED, so a profile using
several colors keeps that pattern intact and simply pulses.

A `baseline` state always pulses, regardless of the `pulse` option: a static
baseline would be pixel-identical to idle and would tell you nothing.

`"current"` and `"profile"` are accepted as aliases. Note that `"gold"` is a
*named color*, not the baseline — use `"baseline"` if you mean "whatever is
already there".

### Device targeting

`include` and `exclude` entries match either a device **type**
(`motherboard`, `gpu`, `keyboard`, …) or a glob against the device **name**
(`ASUS*`, `*X670E*`, `*`). `exclude` wins over `include`.

The default targets interior/ambient hardware only. Keyboards, mice, keypads and
accessories are deliberately left alone: their lighting usually conveys
something already — an Elgato Stream Deck's button icons, for instance — and
hijacking it by default would be obnoxious. Opt in explicitly if you want it:

```jsonc
"devices": { "include": ["*"], "exclude": ["accessory"] }
```

## Scripts

| Command             | What it does                                                             |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `bun run probe`     | Read-only dump of devices, zones, modes; shows what would be targeted     |
| `bun run selftest`  | Writes colors, reads them back from the server, asserts, then restores    |
| `bun run simulate` (`--pulse`, `--hold <ms>`) | Drives the real plugin through every state, so you can preview your palette |
| `bun test`          | Tests for the codec, client, state machine and option parsing             |
| `bun run typecheck` | `tsc --noEmit` over src, scripts and tests                                |

`selftest` and `simulate` change your lighting while they run and restore it
afterwards.

## How it works

The OpenRGB SDK is a binary TCP protocol. This plugin implements the parts it
needs directly, with no runtime dependencies.

A few details that are easy to get wrong, all verified against the OpenRGB
sources and confirmed against real hardware by `scripts/selftest.ts`:

- `RGBColor` is `0x00BBGGRR`, so the little-endian byte order is R, G, B, 0
- In `UPDATELEDS` and `UPDATEMODE`, the leading `data_size` field **counts
  itself**, and equals the packet header's size field
- Below protocol 6, `mode.value` is a device-internal field that must be
  round-tripped back to the server verbatim when updating a mode
- Protocol 5 has no ACK packets, so writes are fire-and-forget

Per-LED color only applies in a direct/custom mode, so the plugin switches the
device into its `Direct` mode if it is not already there, and switches back on
restore. Brightness is applied by scaling RGB in software, because `Direct`
modes commonly report no hardware brightness range at all.

Robustness is a hard requirement: the plugin must never break opencode. If
OpenRGB is not running, is restarted, or misbehaves, every operation degrades to
a silent no-op and the client reconnects in the background with backoff.

### Events

The plugin subscribes to exactly the events that can change the lighting, so it
stays off the firehose of streaming text and step events:

| Event                       | Effect                            |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| `session.status`            | `busy` / `retry` / `idle`         |
| `session.idle`              | session is finished               |
| `session.retry.scheduled`   | a retry is pending                |
| `session.execution.failed`  | raises the error state (10s hold) |
| `permission.asked`          | a prompt is waiting for you       |
| `permission.replied`        | clears that prompt                |
| `session.deleted`           | forgets the session entirely      |

### Restoring on exit

Under opencode 2 the plugin restores from the cleanup function returned by
`setup`, which runs when the plugin unloads. That is an ordinary async context,
so queued socket writes reach OpenRGB normally.

The synchronous write path remains for abrupt teardown. `socket.write` only
*enqueues* data, and if the event loop stops before it flushes, the restore
silently never reaches OpenRGB and the lights stay stuck on the status color —
and the next startup then snapshots that leftover color as the "baseline",
losing the real one. The restore path therefore writes straight to the socket's
file descriptor when it cannot rely on the loop running again. This reaches for
private API (`socket._handle.fd`), so every failure path falls back to a normal
queued write. The plugin also warns at startup if the lighting it captured is
uniformly one of its own status colors, a strong hint that a previous run died
without restoring.

## Limitations

- **Protocol 6 is not implemented.** It lands with OpenRGB 1.0 final and changes
  device addressing to unique IDs. Decoders are version-guarded so the upgrade
  is contained, but until then the client negotiates down to 5.
- **Restore is a startup snapshot.** If you change your lighting in the OpenRGB
  GUI mid-session, the plugin will revert it at the next idle. Restart opencode
  to re-snapshot.
- **A hard kill can still leave the last color showing.** `SIGKILL` or power
  loss gives the plugin no chance to restore. Graceful exits are handled (see
  below).
- **One instance per server.** opencode loads the plugin once per location, but
  the hardware is global, so every instance shares one refcounted controller;
  the last one to unload restores the lighting. Separate opencode *processes*
  would still compete for the hardware.

## Development

```sh
bun install
bun test
bun run typecheck
bun run simulate  # drive real hardware through every state
```

The plugin ships as TypeScript source and opencode loads it directly, so there
is no build step.

The repo's own `opencode.json` wires the plugin locally with `debug: true`, so
running opencode inside this directory loads the working copy.

The entry point (`src/index.ts`) stays thin: it defines the plugin, resolves
options, and pumps the event subscription. The logic lives in
`src/controller.ts` so it is directly importable and testable without a plugin
host — see `test/plugin.test.ts`, which drives the real entry point against a
mock OpenRGB server.

### The root index.ts

opencode resolves a local directory plugin by trying `<dir>/server` and
`<dir>/index`, without consulting `package.json` `main`/`exports`. A plugin
whose only entrypoint is `src/index.ts` resolves to nothing and is dropped
silently, with nothing logged.

Installs by package name do use `exports`, so the root `index.ts` is a
re-export and both resolution paths land on it.

`@opencode/plugin` is imported for types only, so the published package has no
runtime dependencies.

## [0.1.1] - 2026-11-10

### Fixed

- Opened one OpenRGB connection per location rather than one per machine, so a
  single opencode server could run several controllers writing to the same
  devices at once. The shared controller registry was module-level state, but
  opencode gives each location its own module instance, making that scope
  per-location rather than per-process. It now lives on a `globalThis` symbol,
  which is the scope the hardware actually has.

0.1.0 was staged but never released, so no published version carries this bug.

## [0.1.0] - 2026-11-10

Initial release, targeting the opencode 2 plugin API.

### Added

- Ambient status lighting driven by aggregate session state: amber while the
  agent works, yellow on a retry, violet while a permission prompt waits, red
  on failure. Idle restores the lighting captured at startup.
- State is aggregated across all sessions, so subagent and task work keeps the
  lights busy until everything is genuinely finished. The highest priority
  wins: `error` > `permission` > `retry` > `busy` > `idle`.
- `"baseline"` as a state color, breathing the device's *own* startup lighting
  per LED, so an OpenRGB profile keeps its identity and only its intensity
  changes.
- Device targeting by type or name glob, defaulting to interior and ambient
  hardware. Keyboards, mice, keypads and accessories are left alone unless
  explicitly included.
- An OpenRGB SDK client with no runtime dependencies, speaking protocol
  versions 1-5 and negotiating `min(server, 5)`. If OpenRGB is absent,
  restarted, or misbehaving, every operation degrades to a silent no-op and
  the client reconnects in the background with backoff.
- Software brightness scaling, since `Direct` modes commonly report no
  hardware brightness range.
- Configurable pulse, debounce and restore delay, plus a `debug` option and an
  `OPENCODE_OPENRGB_DEBUG` kill switch read in the server process.
- `probe`, `selftest` and `simulate` scripts for inspecting hardware, verifying
  the wire protocol against a real server, and previewing a palette.
- A warning at startup when the captured lighting is uniformly one of the
  plugin's own status colors, which indicates a previous run exited without
  restoring.
